sections.b: 1 Clement, the letter of the church at Rome to the church at Corinth (probably in the 90s; Lake: between 75 and 110), is a long Christian letter built around peace and harmony (eirēnē and homonoia). Its enemy is stasis, the Greek word for faction and civil strife, which the site renders "rebellion" (1 Clement 1:1). It praises the Corinthians' old "peace, deep and rich" (1 Clement 2:2), warns against those "who want peace only as a pretense" (1 Clement 15:1), and calls the church to "run back to the goal of peace that was handed down to us from the beginning" (1 Clement 19:2).

Clement's proof is creation itself. The heavens "submit to him in peace"; day and night never get in each other's way; sun, moon and stars move "in harmony"; the sea stays behind its bars; "The seasons of spring, summer, autumn and winter hand over to one another in peace"; "Even the smallest creatures come together in harmony and peace" (1 Clement 20:1-10). "The great Creator and Master of all things ordered all these to be in peace and harmony" (1 Clement 20:11). The argument joins the Bible's praise of creation (Psalm 104; Job 38) to the Greek idea of the cosmos as an ordered whole: a church at war with itself is out of step with the world God made.

common: 1 Clement's word for the trouble at Corinth, stasis, is the Greek political word for civil strife; its cure, homonoia, is the word for civic concord.

claude.title: Peace as order kept (Claude's reading)
claude.body: In 1 Clement peace is less a feeling than a pattern: everything in its place, doing its own service (the same word, leitourgia, for the winds in 20:10 and the ministers in 40-44). That is why the letter can move from the stars (20) to the Temple service (40-41) to the elders (44) without a break. This is my reading, built on the letter's repeated words.

sections.b: 1 Clement makes jealousy (zēlos) and envy (phthonos) the root of the revolt at Corinth (1 Clement 3:2). It quotes the Wisdom of Solomon, putting "jealousy" where Wisdom has "envy": jealousy is the thing through which "death came into the world" (1 Clement 3:4). Then it lists seven examples from Scripture: Cain, Jacob and Esau, Joseph, Moses, Aaron and Miriam, Dathan and Abiram, David and Saul (1 Clement 4:1-13). Then examples from "our own generation": Peter, Paul, a great multitude of martyrs, and the women called Danaids and Dirces (1 Clement 5:1-6:2). It ends with marriages broken and cities overthrown (1 Clement 6:3-4).
sections.refs: 1 Clement 3:2-4; 1 Clement 4:1-13; 1 Clement 5:1-7; 1 Clement 6:1-4; Wisdom of Solomon 2:24

common: 1 Clement blames jealousy for the deaths of Peter and Paul (1 Clement 5:2-7), a cause the New Testament does not name.

sections.b: Probably in the 90s (Lake: between 75 and 110), the church at Rome wrote that Peter suffered "under unrighteous jealousy" and endured "not one or two but many" hardships, and "Having borne his witness so, he went on to the place of glory owed to him" (1 Clement 5:4). It names neither Rome nor a cross; Rome is implied, because the martyrs who were gathered to these two men suffered "among us" (1 Clement 6:1). Lightfoot argued that "bore his witness" here means martyrdom.

1 Clement 5:5-7 tells of Paul's end: "Seven times he wore chains. He was banished, he was stoned. He became a herald in the East and in the West"; he "came to the far limit of the West" and bore witness "before the rulers". Lightfoot took "the far limit of the West" as Spain, the journey Paul planned (Romans 15:24, 28), which implies a release after the imprisonment of Acts 28; those who hold that Paul died at the end of the Roman captivity must, he says, take it as Rome. The seven imprisonments are in no New Testament book.

1 Clement uses martyreō, "bear witness", of Peter and Paul (1 Clement 5:4, 7). The word had not yet become the fixed term for dying for the faith, but Lightfoot argued that the context shows death is meant. To the two apostles "a great multitude of the chosen was gathered", tortured at Rome (1 Clement 6:1), and women were "hunted down as Danaids and Dirces" (1 Clement 6:2), perhaps forced to act out myths in the arena as they died. Lightfoot connected the multitude with the victims of Nero described by Tacitus (Annals 15.44).

1 Clement speaks of "a great multitude of the chosen" who suffered "many outrages and tortures" at Rome, in the time of Peter and Paul (1 Clement 6:1). Lightfoot saw in it the victims of Nero's persecution after the fire of AD 64, matching Tacitus's multitudo ingens, and he explained the women "hunted down as Danaids and Dirces" (1 Clement 6:2) by the theatrical executions Nero favored.

The church at Rome apologizes for writing late, "misfortunes and calamities have struck us suddenly, one after another" (1 Clement 1:1). Lightfoot read this as Domitian's persecution and dated the letter about AD 95-96. Lake grants that it can then "probably be dated as c. 96 A.D.", but warns that "we know very little about the alleged persecution in the time of Domitian" and dates it safely between 75 and 110.

1 Clement argues that God has always given "a place for repentance" (1 Clement 7:5): Noah preached it and those who listened were saved; Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching (1 Clement 7:6-7); God swore that he wants "the sinner's death" less than "his repentance" (1 Clement 8:2). The blood of Christ "brought the gift of repentance to the whole world" (1 Clement 7:4). The letter quotes Isaiah 1:16-20 and a prophecy in no Bible (1 Clement 8:3), and later the whole of Psalm 51 (1 Clement 18:2-17), as a call to the Corinthian rebels.

1 Clement says "Noah preached repentance, and those who listened were saved" (1 Clement 7:6), and that he "preached a new birth to the world" (1 Clement 9:4), going beyond Genesis with 2 Peter 2:5, which calls him "a herald of righteousness". It adds that the animals went into the ark "together in harmony".

"Jonah preached overthrow to the people of Nineveh. But they repented of their sins and won God's mercy by their pleading, and they received salvation, though they were strangers to God" (1 Clement 7:7), an example of the place for repentance God gives in every generation.

1 Clement makes Enoch the first of those who served God perfectly: "He was found righteous through obedience and was taken away, and his death was never found" (1 Clement 9:3), a turn on the Greek Genesis and Hebrews 11:5, "he was not found".

sections.h: 1 Clement 10 and 17: the friend of God
sections.b: 1 Clement calls Abraham "the friend" who "was found faithful because he obeyed God's words" (1 Clement 10:1), quotes God's promises from the Greek Genesis (1 Clement 10:3-6), and says, "Because of his faith and hospitality he was given a son" (1 Clement 10:7), linking Isaac's birth to the welcome of the three visitors in Genesis 18. Later Abraham is a model of humility: "But I am earth and ashes" (1 Clement 17:2).

Lot "because of his hospitality and godliness, was saved out of Sodom", while his wife "thought differently and was not in harmony with him" and became a pillar of salt, a warning that "the double-minded" bring judgment on themselves (1 Clement 11:1-2).
sections.refs: 1 Clement 11:1-2; Genesis 19:26; Luke 17:32; Wisdom of Solomon 10:6-7

sections.b: 1 Clement retells Joshua 2 and says, "Because of her faith and hospitality Rahab the prostitute was saved" (1 Clement 12:1). The scarlet she hung from her house made it plain "that through the blood of the Lord there will be redemption for all who believe and hope in God", so that "the woman had not only faith but prophecy" (1 Clement 12:7-8). Lightfoot traces this reading of the scarlet cord, as a figure of Christ's blood, on to Justin Martyr, Irenaeus and Origen: "From this time forward it becomes a common type with the fathers."

sections.h: 1 Clement 1 and 10-12: saved by faith and hospitality
sections.b: 1 Clement praises the Corinthians' "magnificent way of welcoming guests" (1 Clement 1:2) and then gives three examples of people saved "because of faith and hospitality": Abraham, who was given a son (1 Clement 10:7), Lot (1 Clement 11:1) and Rahab (1 Clement 12:1, 3). In a port city where Christians traveled through, welcoming them was part of a church's good name.

Against a church revolt, 1 Clement holds up humility (tapeinophrosynē). "Christ belongs to the humble, not to those who lift themselves up over his flock" (1 Clement 16:1); the Lord Jesus came humble, as Isaiah 53 says (1 Clement 16:2-14); "If the Lord was so humble, what should we do" (1 Clement 16:17). Then the humble saints: Elijah, Elisha, Ezekiel, Abraham ("earth and ashes"), Job, Moses, who asked who he was that God should send him, and David with Psalm 51 (1 Clement 17:1-18:17).
sections.refs: 1 Clement 13:1-4; 1 Clement 16:1-17; 1 Clement 17:1-6; 1 Clement 18:1-17; 1 Clement 19:1; Philippians 2:3-8

sections.h: 1 Clement 16: the whole song quoted of Christ
sections.b: 1 Clement 16 quotes Isaiah 53:1-12 entire from the Septuagint, as what the Holy Spirit "had spoken about" the Lord Jesus Christ, to show that he came "humble" (1 Clement 16:2-14), and adds Psalm 22:6-8 as Christ's own words (1 Clement 16:15-16). The Greek differs from the Hebrew in many lines: "as of a little child" for "like a little shoot", "carries our sins" for "our sicknesses he carried", "the Lord handed him over for our sins".

1 Clement calls God "the Father and Maker of the whole world" (1 Clement 19:2) and calls him "The great Creator and Master of all things" (1 Clement 20:11), and gives a hymn to creation in order: heavens, day and night, stars, earth, deeps, sea and ocean, "the worlds beyond it", seasons, winds and springs, all keeping "peace and harmony" (1 Clement 20:1-11).

1 Clement opens with one church writing to another: "The church of God that lives as a resident alien in Rome, to the church of God that lives as a resident alien in Corinth" (1 Clement 1:0). It praises Corinth's past: no rebellion or split, a deep peace, the Spirit poured out on all, a church that submitted to its leaders (1 Clement 1:3-2:8). The portrait is drawn to shame a few who had broken that peace (1 Clement 1:1).

1 Clement introduces seven short sayings with "let us keep in mind the words of the Lord Jesus" (1 Clement 13:1-2): "Show mercy, so that mercy will be shown to you. Forgive, so that you will be forgiven ..." Each is close to Matthew 5-7 or Luke 6, but the set is in no Gospel in this form, and "The kindness you show will be shown to you" has no exact Gospel parallel. Lightfoot thought Clement quoted Matthew and Luke loosely, so that "the hypothesis ... that Clement derived the saying from oral tradition or from some lost Gospel, is not needed". Polycarp to the Philippians 2:3 has a similar list. 1 Clement 2:1 also echoes the saying of Acts 20:35.
sections.refs: 1 Clement 13:1-2; 1 Clement 2:1; Matthew 5:7; Matthew 7:1-2; Luke 6:31-38; Acts 20:35; Polycarp to the Philippians 2:3

sections.h: 1 Clement 4: jealousy and the first murder
sections.b: 1 Clement quotes Genesis 4:3-8 from the Greek, with its reading "If you made your offering rightly but did not divide it rightly, have you not sinned?" (1 Clement 4:4), and draws one lesson: "jealousy and envy led to a brother's murder" (1 Clement 4:7).

1 Clement says "Jealousy sent Dathan and Abiram down living into Hades, for they had risen in rebellion against Moses, God's attendant" (1 Clement 4:12), the first of its uses of the rebellion in Numbers 16 as a warning to Corinth.

A Christian figure drawn from an Old Testament object, which Lightfoot says "becomes a common type with the fathers": the scarlet Rahab hung from her house made it plain "that through the blood of the Lord there will be redemption" (1 Clement 12:7), so that she had "not only faith but prophecy" (1 Clement 12:8).

sections.h: 1 Clement 4 and 17: Moses rejected, Moses humble
sections.b: 1 Clement uses Moses twice: driven out by his own people's jealousy (1 Clement 4:10, quoting Exodus 2:14) and opposed by Dathan and Abiram (1 Clement 4:12); and as a model of humility, "faithful in all his house", who said at the bush, "Who am I, that you send me?" (1 Clement 17:5).
sections.refs: 1 Clement 4:10-12; 1 Clement 17:5-6; Exodus 2:14; Exodus 3:11; Exodus 4:10; Numbers 12:7

sections.b: "What shall we say of David, who was given a good witness?" 1 Clement joins Psalm 89:20 and 1 Samuel 13:14, as Acts 13:22 does, and then quotes Psalm 51:1-17 from the Greek: even the man God chose confessed his sin (1 Clement 18:1-17).
